summary: One-to-one correspondence for ages 4–6: assigning exactly one number word to each object while counting, which requires both tagging (one touch = one word, in synchrony) and keeping track (partitioning the set into already-counted vs not-yet-counted). The central learning mechanism is making that partition visible and manipulable — physically moving or tapping each counted object aside — and progressing arrangements from line → array/circle → scattered, where the child must impose their own tracking. Activities combine performing the count, spotting deliberate miscounts, and progressing to organising a scattered set.
misconceptions: Coordination errors: saying words faster than pointing (or vice versa) → skips or double-counts as the word and the touch drift out of sync.
No tracking strategy on scattered sets → recounting some objects and missing others (the counted/uncounted partition never forms).
Believing pointing without saying (or saying without pointing) still 'counts' — the pairing IS the principle.
Confusing one-to-one correspondence with merely reciting the number-word sequence (stable order): a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' yet not tag objects one-to-one.

activities.title: Feed the squirrel: tap-count a scattered pile
steps: Count a small pile of objects (e.g. 7 acorns to feed a squirrel) by touching each one exactly once, saying one number word with each touch.
Move or tap each counted object into a 'counted' pile/basket so it is clearly separated from the not-yet-counted objects.
Deliberately rush once and double-tap an object; notice the spoken total becomes wrong (e.g. you say 'eight' even though the basket still holds only 7 acorns).
Tidy the scattered objects into a line and recount, touching each once, so it is easier to get a total you can trust.
When the line count gives the right answer, say aloud why: each object got one word and none was counted twice.
activities.insight: The rule 'one word per object, and keep track of what you've already counted' is the very difference between a wrong count and a right one; the counted/uncounted split can be made visible and must be maintained.

activities.title: Did Teddy count right? Spot the miscount
steps: Watch an adult (or a 'count-with-me' character/puppet) count a set of 6 buttons, deliberately pointing to the SAME button twice (…points to one button saying 'four', points to it again saying 'five', ending on 'seven').
Decide whether the count is right and explain how you know.
Point to exactly which button got two number words.
Recount the set yourself, sliding each button aside as it gets its single number word, and give the correct total (6).
activities.insight: Recognising a miscount — and locating the specific object that received two words — shows understanding that the word-to-object pairing IS the rule, not just that the last word spoken is the answer.

activities.title: Count everyday things in structured frames and in daily life
steps: Place one object per cell in a five-frame or ten-frame (or a row of boxes), so each object sits in exactly one slot, then count by touching each filled cell once.
Use fingers as a built-in one-to-one tool: raise one finger per counted object.
Count everyday things through the day — stairs as you climb, claps, plates at the table — one number word per step/clap/plate.
Progress from a line, to an array or circle, to a scattered set that you organise yourself before counting.
activities.insight: One-to-one correspondence applies everywhere and is strengthened by frequent, varied practice; structured slots and fingers support one object per number word (though a child can still skip or double-count cells), and organising a scattered set is the harder test of self-imposed tracking.

checkQuestion: Watch Teddy count these 6 buttons. (Teddy points to one button, says 'four', then points to the SAME button again and says 'five', ending on 'seven'.) Teddy says there are 7 buttons. Is Teddy right? Tell me how you know.
checkAnswer: No — Teddy counted one button twice, so he said too many. Each button should get just one number word. There are 6.
